label: Line chart
question: Revenue changed month by month. Which plot reveals the trend?
why: Time runs left to right and the line joins each month to the next, so the climb from $12K to $45K is obvious at a glance.
pitch: A line chart makes our momentum clear: revenue went from $12K in January to $45K in June.
weakness: A line says 'these points follow each other in order'. That only makes sense when the x-axis is time or another ordered sequence.

label: Pie chart
question: How is NovaTech's first-half revenue split between its four products?
why: Four slices add up to 100% of revenue. A pie answers 'what share does each part take?' and nothing else.
pitch: Core AI brings in 42% of revenue, Flow CRM 28%. The pie shows how the whole is shared.
bestFor: a few parts of one whole
weakness: A pie only works for a handful of slices that add up to a whole. It cannot show change over time, and it gets unreadable with many slices.

label: Scatter plot
question: Do customers who use NovaTech more hours each week stay with us longer?
why: Each dot is one customer: weekly usage on the x-axis, months stayed on the y-axis. The dots form a rising cloud, so heavier users stay longer. Customers have no natural order, so there is nothing to join with a line.
pitch: Every dot is a customer. Heavy users stay longer: roughly 0.8 extra months for every extra weekly hour of usage.
bestFor: the relationship between two numeric variables
weakness: A scatter plot needs two numeric variables to compare. With a single list of values or plain categories there is no relationship to show.

label: Bar chart
question: Which market converts free trials into paying customers best?
why: Bars start at zero and stand side by side, so the eye compares their heights instantly. North America clearly leads.
pitch: North America converts 18.4% of trials, more than three times the rate in MEA.
weakness: Bars compare separate categories. They hide trends over time and they cannot show how values are spread inside a group.

label: Boxplot
question: Our average contract looks great. Are a few whale customers inflating it?
why: The box holds the middle 50% of contracts and the red line is the median ($26.5K). The green triangle, the mean ($43.6K), sits far above it, and the dots are three whale contracts that pull the average up.
pitch: The typical contract is $26.5K, but 3 whale customers lift the average to $43.6K. That is a concentration risk we are managing.
bestFor: spread, the median and outliers of one numeric variable
weakness: A boxplot summarises the distribution of ONE numeric variable. It throws away order, categories and relationships between variables.

label: Area chart
question: How did total revenue build up, and how much did each product add along the way?
why: In a stacked area chart the top edge is total revenue and every coloured band is one product's share of it, month after month.
pitch: The top edge is total revenue. Each band shows what Core AI, Flow CRM and Signal API added every month.
bestFor: how a total builds up from its parts over time
weakness: Filled areas stress volume over time. They make exact comparisons hard and mislead when the categories are not ordered.
